cards.title: Design the offer before you design the popup
cards.summary: A popup form only converts when the incentive behind it is genuinely worth opting in for, so define a strong offer first and pick the form type second.
cards.use_when: You are planning a list-growth popup (email/SMS capture) and need to decide what incentive to put behind it before building anything.
steps: Write out the actual offer you will give in exchange for the email, and make it concrete and valuable ('here is 10% off your order') rather than vague or insider-ish ('sign up for early access').
Test whether you are genuinely willing to deliver that offer to every subscriber — if you are not, pick a different incentive such as free shipping, a dollar amount off, or a free guide.

Only after the offer is set, choose the form type to test: the source's recommended starters are the classic form (straight to email address) and the micro-commit form (a yes/no question before the email field).
Run classic and micro-commit head to head as your first test before adding complexity such as quizzes or gamified forms.
When comparing offers, don't judge only by opt-in rate — check what happens to conversion once those subscribers are on the list, since that is the outcome that matters.
caveats: Source opinion, not a universal law: strong offers beat weak ones, but the source also says copy matters less than the offer.
Platform pricing and template availability change; verify the current interface.

cards.title: Micro-commit popups: ask a yes/no question before requesting the email
cards.summary: Adding a one-question commit step in front of the email field leverages consistency bias and can lift submit rates versus asking for the email immediately.
cards.use_when: You are building a capture popup and want a low-effort form variant to test against a straight-to-email classic form.
steps: Build a first step that asks a single yes/no question tied to the offer, e.g. 'Do you want 10% off your first order?' with buttons like 'Yes please' and 'No thanks'.
Configure the affirmative button action to advance to the next step in the form rather than submitting, so the email field appears only after the click.
Reuse the same visual styling across steps (clone the step in your form builder) so the design stays consistent and you don't rebuild formatting.
In the second step, restate the offer and take the email input; keep to one input per step.
Test this against the classic version. The source's rationale is consistency bias — once someone clicks, they are more likely to finish.
caveats: 'Works better in a lot of scenarios' is the source's claim from practice, not a documented benchmark; results depend on audience.
Adds a click before capture, so measure total subscribers, not just conversion rate.

cards.title: Quiz and gamified popups as alternative capture formats
cards.summary: Quizzes trade a question for the discount and can convert better while collecting segmentation data; spin-to-win and reveal-the-discount forms convert strongly but read as tacky.
cards.use_when: You have already tested classic and micro-commit popups and want additional capture formats, or you need customer preference data for future segmentation.
steps: For a quiz form: ask a question that tells you something useful about the shopper (e.g. which problem they are trying to solve), then present the discount as the earned reward in exchange for that answer.
Tag respondents by their answer in your ESP so you can send segment-specific follow-up emails later.
For a spin-to-win or reveal-the-discount form: make the interaction reveal the reward, then gate claiming it with the email address; the source notes spin-to-win typically lands on the top prize.
Try these formats periodically or rotate them rather than making them your permanent default if your brand positioning depends on a premium look.
Compare formats by opt-in rate and downstream purchase conversion, and remember gamified formats may attract discount-motivated subscribers.
caveats: Source's view: spin-to-win 'converts like crazy' but makes the brand look cheap — a positioning trade-off, not a universal recommendation.
Quiz tools and gamified templates vary by platform; verify which templates your provider currently supports.

cards.title: Hide the X and force a claim-or-decline decision
cards.summary: Making the close button invisible or replacing it with a visible 'no thanks' option forces shoppers to consciously decide on the offer instead of reflex-closing the popup.
cards.use_when: You are designing a popup whose current form is being reflex-closed in the top corner without the offer being read.
steps: Reduce the X icon's visibility (e.g. set its opacity to zero) so the offer is the first thing read.
Add your own secondary button beneath the primary claim button with copy such as 'No thanks, close form' so the shopper can still exit deliberately.
Style the decline button to be visually quiet — blank background, readable text — so it does not compete with the offer.
Keep the offer headline as the largest element on the form and reduce surrounding copy so it is unmistakably the focus.
Keep the required legal SMS consent language small (source suggests roughly size 8) rather than letting it dominate the layout.
caveats: Hiding the exit can frustrate shoppers; the source frames it as improving conversion but notes to keep an explicit decline path.
Accessibility and platform policies may restrict or dislike hidden close controls — check your provider and local requirements.

cards.title: Mobile popup build: single-step capture with email then SMS as a separate step
cards.summary: A high-converting mobile popup keeps one input per step, telegraphs the offer, and sequences email capture before SMS rather than stacking both fields together.
cards.use_when: You are configuring a mobile capture popup in your ESP and want a concrete layout order and settings to start from.
steps: Start from a multi-step email and SMS template, then clone it into a mobile-only form so mobile and desktop data can be analyzed separately.
Set targeting to display on mobile only so the same design is not distorted across devices.
Step 1: email opt-in with the offer as the hero headline; Step 2: phone number for SMS; Step 3: a success message with the discount code and a 'start shopping' style button.
Do not place email and SMS inputs on the same step — the source states this hurts conversion.
In the success step, tell SMS subscribers to confirm on their device and mention that anyone who skips SMS still enters the email welcome flow, so email subscribers are not lost.
Check the success step has a working close/continue button since the X may be hidden.
caveats: Different ESPs name steps and templates differently; tutorial videos referenced in the source may be outdated.
The source's recommended form dimensions (roughly 750x500 on mobile) are a starting point for testing, not a proven optimum.

cards.title: Desktop popup design: go bigger, use a side image, keep one offer
cards.summary: On desktop, a larger popup with a product image on the side and a single clear offer generally converts better than fly-outs or small embeds, at some cost to shopping experience.
cards.use_when: You are designing the desktop version of a capture popup and deciding on size, layout and imagery.
steps: Clone your mobile form into a desktop-only version, then set targeting to display on desktop only.
Use a popup (or a larger custom size) rather than a fly-out, since the source reports fly-outs as less effective.
Use a product or lifestyle image on one side of the form. The source says 'right image' was tested as working best, but recommends testing left, right and no image.
Compress any image before uploading to avoid a slow-loading form.
Verify the layout holds after swapping images, since uploads can reset sizing and formatting.
Ask whether you are willing to trade some browsing experience for a more prominent form; source says bigger forms generally convert better but are more intrusive.
caveats: 'Right image works best' is the source's testing experience, not a universal rule — test it.
Large popups can increase bounce for shoppers mid-browse; consider timing and frequency alongside size.

cards.title: Form targeting: delay, frequency and avoiding exit-intent
cards.summary: Fire popups on a time delay roughly 4-12 seconds after arrival, set a multi-day suppression window after a close, and avoid showing immediately or relying on exit intent.
cards.use_when: You are setting the trigger and frequency rules for a popup and deciding when it appears and re-appears.
steps: Do not show the form immediately on load; the source recommends against it.
Set the trigger to a time-on-page delay rather than exit intent, which the source says misfires and isn't very good.
Start with a 4-second delay and test upward toward 12 seconds.
Set a frequency rule so that after someone closes the form, it does not reappear for several days — the source uses about 5 days as an example.
Restrict the form to the device type it was designed for (mobile-only or desktop-only) so each version's data stays clean.
Advance the delay gradually and compare total submits, not just conversion rate, when choosing a final value.
caveats: Time delay and frequency values are the source's starting heuristics; the right values depend on traffic volume, page speed and audience.
Some platforms offer scroll-depth and page-count triggers as alternatives the source did not recommend over a time delay.

cards.title: Popup form QA checklist before launch
cards.summary: A short pre-launch checklist covering inputs per step, timing, load speed, size, copy length, offer prominence and close-button design catches the common conversion killers.
cards.use_when: You have built a popup and are about to publish it; use this to catch obvious issues before sending traffic.
steps: Confirm only one input is requested per step — never email and SMS together.
Confirm the time delay sits in the roughly 4-12 second range.
Confirm the form loads instantly with no lag when it fires.
Confirm the form covers at least about 75% of the screen so the offer is not easily ignored.
Trim body copy to under about 10 words on the form.
Confirm the offer itself is the largest visual element.
Confirm there is no visible dismissive X, or replace it with a close-form button / an unclear X placement so the shopper makes a decision.
Verify close functionality works on every step, including the success step, so users are not trapped.
caveats: The source presents these as a strong starting checklist for testing, not a guarantee of performance; a strong offer can compensate for one missed item.
'Covers 75% of screen' and 'under 10 words' are the source's heuristics, not measured benchmarks.

cards.title: Seven A/B tests to run on popup forms, in rough priority order
cards.summary: Test offer first, then form type, close functionality, time delay, imagery, copy and color — but judge delay tests on total submits rather than conversion rate.
cards.use_when: You have a live popup form and need a testing backlog ordered by likely impact on subscriber volume and revenue.
steps: Offer first (highest leverage): test 10% off versus $10 off versus free shipping versus a free guide, and include a mystery-offer variant; evaluate both opt-in rate and post-opt-in purchase conversion.
Form type second: test popup versus full-page versus fly-out, and test variations within your chosen type.
Close functionality third: test a close-form button versus an X, and test where the close control sits.

Time delay fourth: compare 4 seconds versus 12 seconds. Judge by total submits, not conversion rate — a 30-second delay may show a higher conversion rate but far fewer total subscribers because few visitors stay that long.
Image content fifth: test different photos and placements; on mobile consider whether an image belongs as the form background.
Copy sixth: test longer versus shorter copy and different phrasing ('unlock my offer' versus 'you've got 10% off').
Colors last: simpler color palettes tend to produce better opt-ins than busy ones.
caveats: The source recommends running a test every couple of days; that cadence requires enough traffic to reach a read.
The illustrative comparison (3% to 4% opt-in on 10,000 visitors equals roughly 100 extra subscribers a month) is arithmetic, not a performance promise.

cards.title: Popup platform choice: built-in ESP forms versus a specialist tool
cards.summary: Your ESP's native popup builder is usually good enough to start, but a dedicated popup platform typically performs better at an added monthly cost.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to build capture forms inside your email platform or subscribe to a dedicated popup tool.
steps: If your ESP is also your email sender, start with its native form builder and templates, then realistically customize them for ecommerce rather than using the default template as-is.

If popups are a meaningful growth channel and budget allows, evaluate a dedicated popup platform (the source cites one at roughly $100/month) and compare opt-in performance against your current forms.
When evaluating a specialist vendor, ask whether they will build your first forms for you as part of onboarding, and confirm what the editor can customize.
Inside a specialist editor, expect to edit copy, images and each step separately; formatting may need manual padding/spacing fixes per device view.
Set targeting (e.g. anonymous visitors) and a time-on-page trigger such as 4 seconds, then preview locally and on your live site before publishing.
Confirm any discount code referenced in the form is created in your store, or the form may fail to deliver the incentive.
caveats: Pricing, free tiers and editor features change frequently — verify current pricing and interface before committing.
The source states it has seen strong ROI from the specialist platform but does not provide a verified benchmark; treat this as testimonial, not proof.

cards.title: Flows versus campaigns: what each is for and how to split revenue
cards.summary: Flows fire automatically when a shopper completes a trigger action and handle personalization across the journey; campaigns are manual sends to the list.
cards.use_when: You are planning your email program structure and deciding how much revenue to expect from automated sequences versus one-off sends.
steps: Define flows as sequences triggered by a specific shopper action (site visit, product view, add to cart, checkout start, purchase, long lapsed purchase); once activated they fire automatically for every qualifying shopper.
Define campaigns as manually created, manually sent emails to your list.
Set up flow triggers through your ecommerce platform integration so events (cart abandonment, purchase) fire the sequence automatically.
Aim for a rough balance — the source suggests targeting roughly 50% of revenue from flows and 50% from campaigns.
Prioritize personalization: different customers are at different journey stages and should receive different information, which is the core advantage of flows over blasts.
Treat this as ongoing work: flows need updating as brand, trends and customer base change.
caveats: The 50/50 split is the source's heuristic, not a calculation derived from data presented here.
Any revenue contribution figures quoted by the source are testimonials from its own client work, not forecasts for your store.

cards.title: The six baseline flows to build first, in order
cards.summary: Nail the basics — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before investing in advanced cross-sell or upsell automations.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which automated email flows to build or fix next, and whether to invest in advanced segmentation or upsell logic.
steps: Welcome flow: 8 emails for new subscribers.
Site abandon flow: 1 email for someone who visited the site and left without deeper action.
Browse abandon flow: 5 emails for someone who viewed a product and left.
Cart abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who added to cart and left.
Checkout abandon flow: 6-8 emails for someone who started checkout and left.
Post-purchase flow: sequence after a purchase.
Win-back flow: for customers who purchased months ago and have gone quiet.

Audit your existing flows against these basics before adding advanced cross-sell, upsell or split tests — the source describes a case where a brand wanted advanced automations while the welcome flow was a single email and cart abandonment was not set up correctly.
caveats: Email counts per flow are the source's recommended structure; your optimal counts depend on catalog, price point and purchase frequency.
The described revenue improvement for one brand (roughly $45k to $133k in a month after fixing basics) is a case example, not a promised result.

cards.title: Build flows in a mobile-first multi-step pattern you can clone across devices
cards.summary: Build the mobile popup first, clone it for desktop, and keep each step focused on one input so both versions can be measured separately.
cards.use_when: You are implementing capture forms across device types and want a repeatable build process rather than two independent designs.
steps: Build the mobile version first with the step sequence you want (micro-commit, email, SMS, success), then clone the form and convert the clone to desktop-only.
Set display rules per clone so mobile and desktop data are analyzed separately rather than as one blended report.
Ask your SMS platform how phone numbers collected in your ESP form flow into their system — the source notes SMS may live on a separate platform.
If you want a micro-commit variant, clone the form again and move the new question step to the front, deleting the email field from that step.
In a specialized popup platform, customize each step's copy and imagery individually, and check that padding and layout are re-applied after any image swap.
Preview both versions before publishing and confirm each step's button actions are correct (advance step versus submit form).
caveats: SMS and ESP integration specifics vary widely by platform and country regulations; verify consent language requirements.
Tutorials referenced in the source may not match current platform interfaces.
